problems.rationale: Acceptance is one no-sorry Lean theorem that every cyclic tag system embeds in Rule 110, with the ether, glider catalogue and collision table as lemmas rather than assumptions. The cyclic-tag module and the collision audit have the largest completion-times-settle products, and neither artifact is that theorem, so they are not a lower bound on the criteria. A logged mismatch on a required collision, or a kernel-checked bisimulation through one tag step, would move this; a month covers layers of the table, not the chain the criteria name.

approaches.note: The light-cone lemma is short, but Cook's glider spacings make the full emulation theorem a long proof the proposer already says will not finish in a month.
Bit-parallel emulation of small tag systems is in reach, while a de Bruijn search out to period 200 and width 100 is not, and an audit still does not prove universality.
There is no tile grammar of Cook's construction in the slice, and unbounded gaps are exactly the failure the proposer names.
This is the same refinement chain as the modular proof, and it still needs a machine-readable phase table nobody has logged.
A bounded collision search can emit certificates, but the proposer notes that completeness past those bounds is a separate mathematical argument.
The table is a finite case analysis the kernel can block into lemmas, and the risk is proof size rather than a missing idea.
Cyclic-tag simulation of Turing machines is classical Lean and never mentions Rule 110, so it can be finished without settling the cellular-automaton theorem.
The bisimulation is forbidden to re-check collisions and still depends on a compiler invariant the proposer says a month will not finish.

problems.rationale: The criteria ask for a Lean construction on a finite-support or eventually periodic tape, or a proof that every such tape is decidable, and both are open. The largest completion-times-settle product is the bounded period-and-grammar search, and that search's own statement says exhaustion does not refute conventional universality. A closed macro-transition inside the stated period bound, or one invariant proved for every period, would move this; another eleven months of the same censuses would not.

approaches.note: A census of regular invariants up to small periods is a computation; a uniform decidability theorem for every eventually periodic tape is the open part.
Replacing Smith's tape with a periodic refuel gadget is a search the proposer says may be far too large, and a candidate still has to be proved in Lean.
Smith's chain is about forty pages, and even a finished tape-complexity bound leaves the periodic-background question open by the approach's own statement.
Nothing in the slice says a universal compiler must use a short period or a local tag encoding, so exhaustion only kills one family.
The bounded-crossing lemma is conjectural, and the proposer notes that runs of 10^9 steps cannot establish decidability.
Non-periodicity of one explicit tape is a smaller lemma than universality, but the public Lean notes are described as still having open items.
No finite invariant for machine 596440 is given, and the theorem has to hold for every period and center length.
The grammar and the period cap are explicit, so the search can be logged, and a hit of 100 tag steps is not a universality proof.

problems.rationale: No logged route yet emulates a universal system in Rule 54, and the problem's falsifier says new gates leave the question open. The collision census of the 2006 catalogue has the largest completion-times-settle product, and a census that finds gates without a tag append is the partial result the criteria exclude. Finding a cyclic-tag append that survives adversarial compositions, or a potential that falls on every collision, would move this.

approaches.note: The glider table can be computed, but a conditional append reaction among small gliders is exactly what has been missing since the 2006 gates.
A decreasing potential would only rule out finite seeds on the ether, and the proposer says periodic program streams escape that argument.
The cycle-enumeration idea is sound, but de Bruijn graphs at period 24 are far past kernel checking, so only a small period bound is realistic.
Phase-restoring fanout and conditional production are the same missing reactions, and failure of this architecture is not a non-universality proof.
A finite particle quotient is a conjecture, and even a finite-defect theorem would leave arbitrary initial configurations open.
Pair collisions of a named catalogue out to separation 256 are a finite double simulation, and the approach itself counts gates without a tag append as failure to settle universality.
No conservation law of this strength is in the slice, and an invariant that still allows an arbitrary tape would not refute universality.
The published gate collisions are a short kernel check, but the monoid may be too large to close, which the proposer calls an inconclusive stop.

problems.rationale: A proof of non-periodicity, density one half, or a general linear-effort bound is open, and the weaker acceptance bar is a new conditional theorem or a proved period past every published check. The largest completion-times-settle product is a restricted-automaton non-automaticity result, which is not one of the three prize statements and is not that weaker bar. A conditional hypothesis strictly weaker than a second periodic column, or a certified prefix longer than the prize-page horizon, would move this.

approaches.note: Jen's theorem is a finite formalization, and the new single-column statement the decisive result also demands is the part nobody has proved.
The swarm as described has simulation previews, not 10^4 GPU-hours, and the approach itself says the output is evidence rather than a proof.
Unsatisfiability for small base-k automata is a finite SAT job, and it does not prove any of the three prize statements.
Excluding periods and preperiods only up to 10^5 does not beat the published million-step checks the acceptance criteria require a new bound to pass.
The algebraic attack needs an invariant connecting left-permutivity to the single seeded column, and the slice does not contain one.
Blocked Lean replay can certify a modest prefix, and the approach fails by its own rule if that prefix does not exceed the published horizon.
Surjectivity and Bernoulli invariance are standard, and equidistribution of the single-seed orbit is the open step the decisive result requires.
Refuting 2-automaticity past a certified prefix needs a distinct kernel sequence at arbitrary scale, which the approach lists as the missing lemma.

problems.rationale: The criteria need a necessary-and-sufficient n=3 theorem and an exhaustive table for n=3 and n=4. The largest completion-times-settle product is the classical n=2 sign list plus equal-diffusion impossibility, which those criteria do not ask for, so it is not a lower bound. A complete n=3 partition with rational witnesses, or a pattern that is potentially stable, not sign-stable, and still Turing-incapable, would move this; exhaustive n=4 certificates are what a year adds and still may not finish.

approaches.note: The n=3 case split is classical once Routh–Hurwitz is formalized, and Mathlib does not already contain that root criterion.
Capable patterns fall to rational witnesses quickly, and the approach fails if CAD or nlsat times out on a substantial incapable set, including at n=4.
The embedding lemma needs spectral perturbation that the proposer says Mathlib lacks, and it does not characterize n=3.
Exact quantifier elimination on every canonical 3-node pattern is the right sentence, and translating those certificates into Lean is the missing piece.
A stratified sample through n=8 can bound a fraction, and the proposer says sampling cannot settle the almost-all conjecture.
Equal diffusion in every dimension and the two classical n=2 patterns are short Hurwitz proofs, and they are not the n=3 classification the criteria demand.
Interval branch-and-bound on all 19683 patterns can leave more than the allowed one percent unresolved, which the approach counts as a failed census.
Two thousand n=4 draws with a hundred rate samples is a small computation, and the pre-registered interval can easily cover both sides of 0.9.

problems.rationale: The criteria are three Lean theorems — the regression identity, the additive rule, and a frequency-dependent counterexample — plus a map onto the 2010–2011 papers. The largest completion-times-settle product is the counterexample family alone, which does not include the regression identity or that map, so the problem probability sits just below it. A compiled development of all three theorems would move this; a Moran sign table by itself would not.

approaches.note: Price's identity and the normal equations are standard, and the approach fails as a resolution if the mapping only documents an equivocation.
The counterexamples are rational instances of a two-player game, and norm_num can discharge them once the closed form is proved.
Exact fixation on small graphs is feasible, and Monte Carlo at larger N can leave signs inside the neutral interval, which is the named failure.
This is the same three-way split as the Price-equation module, with the extra demand that a searched countermodel survive consistent definitions of relatedness.
Populations of size at most 8 are an exact rational enumeration, and the taxonomy can still depend on arbitrary regression conventions.
The three readings have disjoint hypotheses and are formalizable, and genealogical relatedness in the additive case is the fiddly lemma.
A seven-state Moran chain with rational fitness is a closed-form matrix, so the sign table can be logged without being the Lean development.
The stationary distribution of that same chain is immediate, and the pre-registered 0.05 gap from the ESS may simply not appear for this payoff.

problems.rationale: Acceptance asks for a classification of the cylindrical Douady–Couder map, including the Lucas branch, with a proof, and basin maps that match it. The largest completion-times-settle product is the continued-fraction lattice theorem, and that approach states that it does not classify dynamical attractors. A Morse graph or an interval-Newton partition with no unclassified recurrent set on a stated interval would move this.

approaches.note: Interval Newton plus a Conley–Morse graph would meet the cylindrical criteria, and the swarm has no logged validated-numerics stack for the discontinuities near bifurcations.
Mathlib already has continued fractions and Fibonacci numbers, and the approach states that these lattice theorems do not classify dynamical attractors.
A 10^5-run multinomial comparison is a data test the organisms layer can host, and the sunflower counts may not separate Lucas heads from other non-Fibonacci heads.
The decisive result demands uncovered measure below 10^-6, and the proposer says the validated-numerics infrastructure for the placement rule is missing.
Sampling 100000 seeds per stratum can build a basin atlas, and the approach itself says simulation cannot prove full measure.
Interval Newton on the Atela–Golé–Hotton grid is a concrete certificate, and a grid is not yet a theorem for every parameter in the interval.
The 2003 stability argument is a long real-analysis paper, and the proposer says a month may finish the labeling and not the estimates.
Two hundred parameters times five hundred seeds on the disc is an ordinary simulation, and it can falsify a list without proving the cylindrical classification.

problems.rationale: The criteria are a pre-registered comparative test, using a diversity compilation and GBIF range proxies, that actually verdicts whether linked selection closes the gap. The slope of log diversity on log census size can be fit from the Leffler and Buffalo tables; public recombination maps cover few of those species, so the linked-selection term is the shared blocker. Generic forward simulations do not remove it, because the slice says direct simulation at large census size is infeasible. A residual slope from at least eight species with real maps, or a pre-registered regime whose diversity curve misses the empirical slope at both ends, would move this.

approaches.note: GBIF ranges and a phylogenetic slope are in the organisms layer, and recombination maps exist for too few species to test the linked-selection prediction on the full set.
Pedigree mutation rates exist for dozens of vertebrates, and the matched diversity set can fall under the thirty species the approach calls underpowered.
SLiM up to 10^7 with an extrapolation to 10^12 is the proposer's own missing step, and sweep interference makes the upper bound model-dependent.
The design demands thirty measured recombination maps and one hundred fifty range proxies, which the proposer says are sparse outside model organisms.
Window-level tests need harmonized callsets for twenty species, and the failure mode is held-out R^2 below 0.1 in more than half of them.
The nested model on Leffler diversity, published census size and a GBIF bounding box can be pre-registered, and this approach deliberately does not fit linked selection.
The marker floor is honest, and the approach is written to stop as underpowered if fewer than eight species have a real map.
Three frozen regimes on a census-size grid can be simulated at modest N, and the approach does not use species-specific maps, so a match would still be generic.

problems.rationale: The criteria need both a phylogenetically controlled verdict and a Lean derivation of the West–Brown–Enquist 3/4 with its hypotheses named. The largest completion-times-settle product is the finite-generation numerical check, which that approach says reports only the algebra and is neither of the two required artifacts. An interval that excludes 2/3 or 3/4, or a clade model that beats the power law by the pre-registered margin, together with the compiled hypotheses, would move this.

approaches.note: Several hundred mammal species can separate 2/3 from 3/4 if the relation is linear, and the verdict can still flip with basal-versus-resting inclusion rules.
The finite-N geometric series and the 3/4 limit are Mathlib-scale lemmas once the four network hypotheses are written as hypotheses.
A hierarchical model across domains can refute a single exponent, and the prokaryote and protist samples are the ones the approach says may leave the heterogeneity interval wide.
Family-held-out comparison of five models is a concrete PGLS design, and it fails if both 2/3 and 3/4 remain inside the common-slope interval.
Separating area preservation from the 3/4 conclusion is a shorter proof than the data analysis, and it does not say whether organisms meet the hypotheses.
The PanTHERIA columns, the missing-value code and the hundred Upham trees are specified, and geographic temperature is correctly excluded as a body-temperature control.
A no-sorry 3/4 from named branching hypotheses, plus one consistency lemma for the critiqued service volume, is a bounded formalization.
Generations 2 through 24 of two explicit networks are a short exact calculation, and the approach says it checks the algebra rather than real mammals.
